passage.title: The Three-Thousand-Mile Compass
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Each fall, millions of monarch butterflies leave northern fields to begin a remarkable trip. Though each bug weighs less than a dime, its bright wings carry it three thousand miles south to the hills of central Mexico. Even more surprising, no single monarch ever makes the round trip twice. The monarchs flying south in fall are the great-grandchildren of the ones that left Mexico in the spring. Yet without an older guide to lead the way, the flock reaches the exact same groves of fir trees year after year.

For decades, scientists asked how a bug with a brain the size of a pinhead could steer such a straight path. Studies showed that monarchs rely on a built-in sun compass. Special cells in the butterfly's eyes track the spot of the sun in the sky. Because the sun moves from east to west each day, a simple sun tracker would send the bug in circles unless it also knew the time. Throughout the long autumn flight, the shifting angles of the afternoon sun are constantly adjusted by an internal clock hidden in the butterfly's antennae.

To test this idea, teams placed monarchs in a flight box where indoor lights shifted the day by six hours. When the feeler clocks were out of step with the real sky, the bugs turned the wrong way. Next, teams painted a harmless black coat on the feelers to block light. Right away, the bugs lost their sense of time and drifted off course. Clear enamel paint let sunlight reach the feeler clocks and helped the butterflies steer southwest again.

Still, a sun compass cannot explain how monarchs fly straight when thick gray clouds hide the sky. Scientists found that the insects carry a backup tool tuned to Earth's magnetic pull. Tiny cells in the feelers and eyes sense the tilt of magnetic lines running from pole to pole. When the sun is obscured by heavy cloud cover, this magnetic sense acts like an unseen slope map that points the bug south.

Once the monarchs reach the cool peaks of Mexico, a new cue tells them to stop and rest on the fir boughs. Cold hill air and short winter days flip a switch inside them, steering them back north in the spring. By blending sun angles, body clocks, and magnetic sensors, these fragile bugs endure one of the longest journeys on Earth.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"Throughout the long autumn flight, the shifting angles of the afternoon sun are constantly adjusted by an internal clock hidden in the butterfly's antennae."

In this sentence, what actually performs the action of adjusting the sun's angles?

options.text: The afternoon sun moving from east to west
options.childFeedback: The afternoon sun moves across the sky, creating the shifting angles—it isn't the clock inside the butterfly that adjusts for those angles!

options.text: A team of scientists watching from a hill in Mexico
options.childFeedback: Scientists aren't mentioned in that sentence from Paragraph 2; it is the internal clock hidden in the butterfly's antennae that does the adjusting.

options.text: The long autumn flight across the northern fields
options.childFeedback: 'Throughout the long autumn flight' only tells WHEN this happens, not what tool adjusts the sun's shifting angles.

options.text: An internal clock hidden in the butterfly's antennae
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, the passive verb 'are constantly adjusted by' points to 'an internal clock hidden in the butterfly's antennae' as what adjusts for the sun's shifting angles.

questions.provingSentenceText: Throughout the long autumn flight, the shifting angles of the afternoon sun are constantly adjusted by an internal clock hidden in the butterfly's antennae.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, the passive verb 'are constantly adjusted by' points to 'an internal clock hidden in the butterfly's antennae' as what adjusts for the sun's shifting angles.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive construction, 'the shifting angles of the afternoon sun' receives the action. The true grammatical actor comes after the preposition 'by': 'an internal clock hidden in the butterfly's antennae' (Option B).
questions.retryHint: Look right after 'are constantly adjusted by' in Paragraph 2 to see what adjusts the sun's shifting angles.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 4:

"When the sun is obscured by heavy cloud cover, this magnetic sense acts like an unseen slope map that points the bug south."

What does the word "obscured" mean as it is used in this sentence?

options.text: Measured carefully with a laboratory stopwatch
options.childFeedback: Heavy clouds in the sky don't measure the sun with a stopwatch! Paragraph 4 says thick gray clouds hide the sun from view.

options.text: Heated to a much brighter glow during the afternoon
options.childFeedback: Heavy gray cloud cover blocks sunlight rather than heating the sun to a brighter glow! 'Obscured' means hidden from view.

options.text: Hidden from view or blocked so it cannot be seen
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, 'obscured' means hidden from view or blocked so it cannot be seen. Earlier in the same paragraph, the author gives the clue that 'thick gray clouds hide the sky.'

options.text: Painted with a coat of clear enamel polish
options.childFeedback: Scientists painted clear enamel onto the butterflies' feelers in Paragraph 3, not onto the sun in Paragraph 4! 'Obscured' means hidden by clouds.

questions.provingSentenceText: When the sun is obscured by heavy cloud cover, this magnetic sense acts like an unseen slope map that points the bug south.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 4, 'obscured' means hidden from view or blocked so it cannot be seen. Earlier in the same paragraph, the author gives the clue that 'thick gray clouds hide the sky.'
questions.parentExplanation: Earlier in Paragraph 4, the author notes that 'thick gray clouds hide the sky.' Therefore, when the sun is 'obscured by heavy cloud cover,' it is hidden from view (Option A).
questions.retryHint: Connect 'obscured by heavy cloud cover' to the clue earlier in Paragraph 4 about what thick gray clouds do to the sky.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 3, why did teams paint clear enamel onto the monarchs' feelers after testing black paint?

options.text: To make the butterflies easier to spot against the dark fir trees in Mexico
options.childFeedback: Clear enamel paint is see-through, so it wouldn't make butterflies easier to spot against dark trees! It was used in Paragraph 3 to let sunlight reach their feelers.

options.text: To prove that blocking light, rather than the paint itself, was what threw off the feeler clocks
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 3, black paint blocked light and threw the monarchs off course, while clear enamel paint let sunlight reach the feeler clocks so they steered southwest again—proving the clocks need light.

options.text: To protect the insects' eyes from strong winds inside the flight box
options.childFeedback: The scientists painted the butterflies' feelers (antennae), not their eyes, and they were testing light and time, not blocking wind.

options.text: To permanently stop all monarchs from flying south during the fall
options.childFeedback: Clear paint didn't stop the monarchs from flying south—Paragraph 3 says it actually helped them steer southwest again!

questions.provingSentenceText: Clear enamel paint let sunlight reach the feeler clocks and helped the butterflies steer southwest again.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 3, black paint blocked light and threw the monarchs off course, while clear enamel paint let sunlight reach the feeler clocks so they steered southwest again—proving the clocks need light.
questions.parentExplanation: When black paint blocked light from the feelers, the monarchs drifted off course. Using clear enamel paint let sunlight reach the feeler clocks and restored accurate steering, proving the clocks need light to keep time (Option A).
questions.retryHint: Compare what happened in Paragraph 3 when black paint blocked light versus when clear paint let sunlight through to the feelers.

questions.prompt: Which piece of evidence does the author use in Paragraph 1 to show that monarch migration must be guided by instinct rather than learned from older butterflies?

options.text: The butterflies flying south in fall are the great-grandchildren of the ones that left Mexico in spring.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 proves that monarchs cannot follow an older guide because no single butterfly makes the round trip twice—the fall flyers are the great-grandchildren of the ones that left Mexico in spring.

options.text: Each monarch butterfly weighs less than a dime when it leaves the northern fields.
options.childFeedback: Weighing less than a dime shows how tiny and fragile each butterfly is, not how it knows the way without an older guide.

options.text: Special cells in the eyes track the spot of the sun in the afternoon sky.
options.childFeedback: Eye cells that track the sun are explained in Paragraph 2, not Paragraph 1, and they describe the sun compass rather than generations.

options.text: Fir trees grow only on the highest mountain peaks in central Mexico.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 mentions the groves of fir trees in central Mexico, but it never claims fir trees grow only there or that trees explain instinct.

questions.provingSentenceText: The monarchs flying south in fall are the great-grandchildren of the ones that left Mexico in the spring.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 1 proves that monarchs cannot follow an older guide because no single butterfly makes the round trip twice—the fall flyers are the great-grandchildren of the ones that left Mexico in spring.
questions.parentExplanation: The author supports the claim that monarchs have no experienced guide by pointing out that no monarch makes the round trip twice; the fall travelers are the great-grandchildren of those that left Mexico in the spring (Option B).
questions.retryHint: Check Paragraph 1 for the detail about how the fall butterflies are related to the butterflies that left Mexico in the spring.

questions.prompt: PART A: Which statement best summarizes how monarch butterflies navigate across North America?

options.text: They follow the scent of fir needles blown northward from Mexico by warm autumn winds.
options.childFeedback: The passage never says monarchs smell fir needles from three thousand miles away; they use sun angles, antennae clocks, and magnetic sensors.

options.text: They combine an eye-based sun tracker, light-sensitive clocks, and a backup magnetic compass to stay on course in any weather.
options.childFeedback: Across the passage, we learn that monarchs steer three thousand miles by combining an eye-based sun tracker, light-sensitive feeler clocks, and a backup magnetic compass for cloudy days.

options.text: They rely solely on Earth's magnetic pull because the sun moves too rapidly across the sky to be useful.
options.childFeedback: Monarchs don't ignore the sun! Paragraphs 2 and 3 explain that their main guide is a sun compass paired with an internal clock, while magnetic pull is a cloudy-day backup.

options.text: They wait on the ground whenever clouds appear because their feelers stop working without direct sunlight.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 explains that monarchs DO keep flying straight when thick clouds hide the sun because their backup magnetic compass points them south.

questions.provingSentenceText: By blending sun angles, body clocks, and magnetic sensors, these fragile bugs endure one of the longest journeys on Earth.
questions.childTip: Across the passage, we learn that monarchs steer three thousand miles by combining an eye-based sun tracker, light-sensitive feeler clocks, and a backup magnetic compass for cloudy days.
questions.parentExplanation: Across Paragraphs 2–5, the passage explains that monarchs combine their sun tracker, their time-keeping clocks, and a backup magnetic field sensor on cloudy days to navigate three thousand miles (Option A).
questions.retryHint: Look at the final sentence of Paragraph 5 to see which three navigation tools monarchs combine on their trip.

questions.prompt: PART B: Which quotation from the passage best supports the correct answer to Question 5?

options.text: "Even more surprising, no single monarch ever makes the round trip twice."
options.childFeedback: This line from Paragraph 1 explains that no single butterfly makes the round trip twice, but it doesn't name the tools they use to navigate.

options.text: "To test this idea, teams placed monarchs in a flight box where indoor lights shifted the day by six hours."
options.childFeedback: This sentence from Paragraph 3 only describes one indoor lab test with shifted lights, leaving out the backup magnetic compass.

options.text: "Once the monarchs reach the cool peaks of Mexico, a new cue tells them to stop and rest on the fir boughs."
options.childFeedback: This detail from Paragraph 5 describes what happens after the monarchs arrive in Mexico, not how they steered their way there.

options.text: "By blending sun angles, body clocks, and magnetic sensors, these fragile bugs endure one of the longest journeys on Earth."
options.childFeedback: This final sentence from Paragraph 5 directly supports Question 5 by naming all three tools—sun angles, body clocks, and magnetic sensors—that guide the monarchs' journey.

questions.provingSentenceText: By blending sun angles, body clocks, and magnetic sensors, these fragile bugs endure one of the longest journeys on Earth.
questions.childTip: This final sentence from Paragraph 5 directly supports Question 5 by naming all three tools—sun angles, body clocks, and magnetic sensors—that guide the monarchs' journey.
questions.parentExplanation: Option C directly proves Part A by summarizing the three biological systems—sun angles, body clocks, and magnetic sensors—that guide the monarch migration.
questions.retryHint: Check the final sentence of Paragraph 5 to see how sun angles, body clocks, and magnetic sensors work together.
